en: Hidden energy users in the kitchen
Calculating the real cost of small appliances
Standby power, phantom loads and smart solutions
Students will identify small kitchen appliances (kettle, toaster, coffee machine), understand their power ratings, and recognise the concept of standby power.
Students will calculate consumption and cost for daily use patterns, compare appliances, and evaluate the impact of standby power.
Students will model total small-appliance energy profiles, analyse phantom loads, evaluate smart plug solutions, and propose household efficiency strategies.

Besides the refrigerator and oven, kitchens contain many smaller electrical appliances: kettles, toasters, coffee machines, blenders, and more. Individually, each one uses relatively little energy. But used together, several times a day, they can add up to a surprising amount.

An often-overlooked issue is STANDBY POWER – the electricity consumed by appliances that are plugged in but not actively in use. A coffee machine displaying the time, a microwave with a glowing clock, or a kettle with an illuminated base all consume standby power continuously.
Small kitchen appliances generally have high power ratings but short usage times. An electric kettle uses 2,000–3,000 W but only runs for a few minutes. The total energy per use is therefore small.
STANDBY POWER typically ranges from 0.5 to 5 W per appliance. This seems negligible, but a device consuming 3 W continuously uses:
3 W × 24 h × 365 days ÷ 1,000 = 26.3 kWh per year
With 5–10 appliances on standby in a kitchen, this can exceed 100–200 kWh per year – equivalent to running a modern refrigerator.
**A coffee machine uses 1,200 W during brewing (5 min) and 3 W on standby (23 h 55 min).**
**Surprisingly, standby accounts for 42% of the daily consumption!**

At this level you will calculate the exact energy consumption and cost of small kitchen appliances, separating active use from standby power. You will discover that standby consumption can rival or exceed active consumption for some appliances.

**What you should already know: You should be able to identify small kitchen appliances and their power ratings, understand the concept of standby power, and know the formula Energy (kWh) = Power (W) × Time (h) ÷ 1,000.**
For appliances with standby power, the total daily energy consumption has two parts:
Total daily kWh = Active kWh + Standby kWh
Active kWh = Active power (W) × Active time (h) ÷ 1,000
Standby kWh = Standby power (W) × Standby time (h) ÷ 1,000

Phantom loads from small appliances represent one of the easiest areas for energy savings in a household. Smart plugs and timed power strips can automatically eliminate standby power. At this level you will model the total phantom load of a kitchen, evaluate smart plug solutions, and analyse the broader environmental impact.
**What you should already know: You should be able to calculate active and standby energy separately, compute standby percentages, and understand the concept of phantom loads.**

A SMART PLUG is a device inserted between the wall socket and the appliance. It can be programmed to cut power completely at certain times, or to switch off automatically after a period of inactivity. Smart plugs typically cost €10–25 each.
The PAYBACK PERIOD for a smart plug depends on:
Payback (years) = Smart plug cost (€) ÷ Annual standby cost saved (€/year)
For appliances with high standby power (3–5 W), payback can be less than one year.
